title: Library schema in PostgreSQL
idea: The library schema maps each Java class to a table and lets PostgreSQL enforce key rules: one open loan per copy, one live reservation per member and title.

analogy.text: A copy's slot in the loan ledger takes one open stamp. A second clerk's stamp is refused.
analogy.breaks: A real ledger can be overwritten; the index refuses at write time.

points: A partial unique index on loan(copy_id) allows only one open loan per copy.
Status columns are TEXT with a CHECK listing the Java enum values.
Every index names the query it serves: free copies, overdue sweep, queue order.
Borrow locks the member row, then takes a free copy with SKIP LOCKED.

steps.caption: Two members borrow the same title at once. Only CP-1 is free.
M-1 selects a free copy `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and locks CP-1.
M-2 runs the same query. SKIP LOCKED skips CP-1 instead of waiting.
No other free copy exists, so M-2 gets zero rows and rolls back with NO_COPY.
M-1 marks CP-1 ON_LOAN and inserts the loan row.
M-1 commits. Even a buggy second insert would hit the partial unique index.

code.title: Tables and constraints
code.caption: The schema on a real PostgreSQL 18, then five bad writes the database refuses by itself, and the overdue query.

walk.text: Book is the title; book_copy holds status. The index serves 'find a free copy of this ISBN'.
Fines are BIGINT minor units with a CHECK that they never go negative.
Due dates are DATE, a calendar day. CHECKs guard renewals, status and date order.
Partial indexes cover only open loans: one per copy, plus the sweep and 'my loans'.
One live reservation per member and title; the queue index orders by created_at.
Print the Postgres error code and constraint name for each refused write.
The overdue sweep query, served by the partial index on due_on.

code.title: Borrow and return transactions
code.caption: Two races decided by the database, then a late return that serves the reservation queue in the same transaction.

walk.text: `tx` runs one transaction; a Refused error rolls back and returns its code.
Lock the member row first, so two borrows by one member check the limit in turn.
Pick a free copy, or one held for this member, skipping rows others have locked.
Mark the copy ON_LOAN, fulfil this member's READY reservation, and insert a 14-day loan.
Return closes the open loan and prices the fine; a second scan finds nothing.
Lock the oldest WAITING reservation and hold the copy for it, or shelve it as AVAILABLE.
Run both races in parallel and print only the sorted outcomes.

pitfalls: Do not trust the service alone; add the partial unique index on open loans.
Lock rows in one fixed order (member, then copy) to avoid deadlocks.
Run the queue hand-off in the return transaction, or a copy can go unclaimed.

quiz.q: What does borrow.mjs print for the last-copy race?
quiz.why: One transaction locks CP-1. The other skips the locked row or sees ON_LOAN, finds no copy, and rolls back.

takeaway: Constraints guard the rules; row locks decide who wins a race.

starters: When should I use SKIP LOCKED instead of waiting on the lock?
Why is due_on a DATE and not a TIMESTAMPTZ?
How would the overdue sweep scale to millions of loans?
